title: A Critical Review of the Common Ownership Literature - Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta
summary: Gerardi-Lowry-Schenone, Atlanta Fed WP 2023-17 / ECGI 943: critical survey of common-ownership literature on measurement, identification and mechanisms; conclude little credible evidence of anticompetitive effects. Abstract-only note. Confirms critique of merger/index-event designs persists to 2023.

title: A Flow-Based Explanation for Return Predictability
summary: Lou (2012 RFS) 'A flow-based explanation for return predictability' (draft July 2012). Builds stock-level demand shocks by aggregating flow-induced trading across all mutual funds holding the stock (expected flow x lagged holdings): documents significant temporary price impact; expected flow-induced trading predicts next-year returns, reversing later; explains fund performance persistence, smart money effect and partly momentum. Relevance: standard flow-induced-trading (FIT) construction and the overlap-based 'all funds holding the stock' aggregation; no horizon dimension. Useful template for neighbour-based instruments and for identifying demand shocks that propagate through overlap, relevant to pivot A identification design. Fetched via LSE-hosted working paper (RFS DOI blocked by Cloudflare).

title: A Model of Multi-Frequency Trade∗
summary: Crouzet, Dew-Becker, Nathanson (2017; later published RFS as Multi-frequency trading) noisy REE model where investors acquire information and trade at a continuum of frequencies; endogenous specialization by frequency; restricting high-frequency trading affects high-frequency price efficiency but not low-frequency; high- and low-frequency investors coexist and profit from each other; holdings forecast returns at the frequency at which they trade. Closest THEORETICAL precedent for horizon heterogeneity as an equilibrium object: horizons are endogenous by information-acquisition specialization, not by network adaptation or peer influence. Means pivot E cannot claim novelty for 'endogenous horizon' per se; the novelty must be the network/peer-adaptation mechanism. Note: this URL was assigned as a 'multi-frequency' paper (not Hortacsu).

title: A new measure for differences of opinions: Institutional trade dispersion
summary: Alldredge & Caglayan (J Banking & Finance 170, 2025). Dispersion in institutions' QUARTERLY TRADES (not horizons) as divergence-of-opinion; increases predict lower future abnormal returns. 13F. Adjacent: dispersion across holders of a stock but of trade direction, not horizon; outcome returns not volatility/liquidity.

title: A Review of the Fractal Market Hypothesis for Trading and Market Price Prediction
summary: Blackledge and Lamphiere (Mathematics 10(1):117, Dec 2021; MDPI review, 46 pp, open access). Frames the FMH against random walk and EMH via self-affine/Levy-stable scaling, fractional calculus and the Generalised Kolmogorov-Feller equation; proposes Levy index plus Lyapunov exponent plus volatility for long-term risk forecasts, and an ML-evolved nonlinear price formula with a Bitcoin case study. Treats the FMH as a time-series scaling model; heterogeneous horizons enter only as narrative motivation (interactions among agents with different horizons produce crashes when broken). No holdings data, no agent or network microfoundation, no formal statistical test of the horizon mechanism. Useful as evidence that the FMH literature is dominated by time-series scaling/econophysics, with the investor-level microfoundation gap still open. Venue is MDPI Mathematics, not a top finance outlet, so reliability moderate.

title: Active trading and (poor) performance: The social transmission channel
summary: Escobar and Pedraza (JFE 150(1), 2023, 139-165), abstract via IDEAS. Outcome: likelihood of starting to trade, purchase of same stocks as classmates, attraction to extreme-return stocks; peer = quasi-randomly assigned classmates in a financial training program; retail. Closeness to A: ADJACENT (peer effects in trading activity, retail, random assignment).

title: American Economic Journal: Microeconomics 2013, 5(3): 69–96
summary: Baccara & Yariv (AEJ: Microeconomics 2013, 5(3):69-96). Game-theoretic model of endogenous peer-group formation: agents choose peers, then contribute to public projects; stable groups must be sufficiently homogeneous in preferences and some heterogeneity can persist as group size grows; with information sharing, stability requires more similarity among extremists than moderates. Provides microfoundation for why homophily (similar types preferentially group) is an equilibrium outcome, supporting the paper's assumption of preferential linking by similar tau. Not investor-specific. Fetched via author-hosted PDF after DOI redirected to AEA login.

title: An Equilibrium Model of Institutional Demand and Asset Prices | Becker Friedman Institute
summary: BFI landing page (abstract only) for Koijen-Yogo demand system: asset demand with rich investor heterogeneity matched to institutional holdings, unique equilibrium prices from market clearing, two identification strategies (coefficient restriction, IV via investment-universe-based instruments), applied to institutions' role in price movements, liquidity, volatility, predictability. Full text is in nber-working-paper-series-12 (JPE 2019). Relevance: the demand-system benchmark a referee will demand for any holdings-based fragility/price-impact claim; latent demand heterogeneity is not horizon-specific and has no peer/network channel.

title: arXiv:1402.2494v2  [q-fin.GN]  28 Aug 2014
summary: Bohlin & Rosvall (2014, arXiv q-fin.GN; Swedish central shareholder register, individual investors not institutions). Builds an investor similarity network (nodes = investors, links = cosine similarity of portfolio vectors), partitions with Infomap community detection, and shows investors in the same community trade more similarly (buy the same stocks) than investors outside it. Establishes holdings-similarity as a predictor of trading behaviour but uses NO horizon/turnover/holding-period variable (grep for horizon/turnover/holding period: zero hits as a variable). Relevant to pivot D as a methodological precedent: cosine portfolio-similarity networks are standard; horizon proximity as a determinant of similarity is not tested here. Individual-investor data; not 13F.

title: arXiv:1907.01119v1  [q-fin.ST]  2 Jul 2019
summary: Wang, Ma, Jiang, Zhou, Sornette (2019, arXiv q-fin.ST). Compares layered ego-network (Dunbar-circle) structure of Ozsoylev et al. (2014) 'empirical investor networks' (EIN: investors linked if they place same-direction orders on same stock-day, Turkish exchange data) with cellphone networks; finds two node groups with 5/15/50/150 layer structure. Marginal relevance: confirms the EIN literature (Ozsoylev, Walden, Yavuz, Bildik, RFS 2014) builds investor networks from co-trading, no horizon variable; low priority.

title: Assessing systemic risk due to ﬁre sales spillover
summary: Assessing systemic risk due to fire sales spillover through maximum entropy network reconstruction (arXiv 1509.00607; Di Gangi, Lillo, Pirino). Reconstructs bank-asset bipartite network when holdings are only partially observed and evaluates fire-sale spillover (Greenwood-Landier-Thesmar style) via maximum-entropy. Relevance: methods lead on network reconstruction/overlap-based spillover; banks not 13F equity; no horizon element. Low-medium priority.

title: Asset Manager Commonality and Portfolio Similarity - Dallasfed.org
summary: Ozdagli-Ryfe, Dallas Fed WP 2515r1 (2025). Life insurers sharing an external asset manager hold more similar portfolios and trades; stronger if manager actively oversees majority of both insurers' assets; grows with duration of sharing; driven by purchases not sales; return-correlation increase small. Design = staggered switches of shared asset manager (manually collected, bond holdings). Closest precedent for shock-style identification of common-manager similarity, but outcome is portfolio similarity, not horizon or turnover; not a closure/merger of the institution itself and bond/insurer specific.

title: Audited absence: dispersion-crash (cc-5), horizon-sorted overlap (cc-6)
summary: Searches and forward-citation audit of Chan-Cheng-Hameed (21 citers, none on crash risk with dispersion); no near-duplicate for dispersion-to-crash and none for horizon-sorted portfolio overlap; closest level/type papers listed.

title: Balakina and Stockler 2025 - Peer Effects in Multi-Layer Networks (BSE NetSci)
summary: Balakina & Stockler (Jan 2025, BSE NetSci conf. paper) 'Peer Effects in Multi-Layer Networks: Evidence from Financial Behavior'. Danish registry data; three peer layers (coworkers, family, neighbours, ~3000 shires) jointly; IV 2SLS with instruments built from third-degree peers' demographics and shock sensitivity (third-degree coworker = coworker of spouse of a coworker), citing Bramoulle et al. 2009, De Paula 2017, Manski 1993. Neighbours strongest, then coworkers, then family; stronger for stocks than funds and for experienced investors; coworkers drive buying, neighbours both buying and selling. Dependent var = indicator of any stock trade (turnover-like), peers' share trading. Model: multi-layer centrality. HOUSEHOLD investors, not institutions; does not examine horizon or overlap networks. Note: BSE paper cited by self as showing peer effects in trading ACTIVITY, an adjacent precedent to horizon peer effects but not institutional.

title: Ben Mbarek 2026 SSRN 7048161: Institutional Ownership Dynamics, Market Behavior, and Stock Price Crash Risk (abstract via Crossref)
summary: French equities 2010-2024: institutional ownership level and reductions raise crash risk (exit channel). Level/change only; no horizon dispersion.

title: Benkraiem et al. 2022 JIFMIM: Investor heterogeneity and negative skewness (abstract-level)
summary: Published version of Zhu skewness WP: short-term institutional ownership level drives negative skewness, long-term reduces it; 'heterogeneity' = horizon type shares, not dispersion. No stock-level dispersion test.

title: Better to stay apart: asset commonality, bipartite network centrality, and investment strategies | Annals of Operations Research | Springer Nature Link
summary: Flori, Lillo, Pammolli (Annals of Operations Research 299, 2021, 177-213; SSRN 3275178 2018). Bipartite fund-asset networks; asset commonality / bipartite centrality; funds with lower commonality (staying apart) perform better. No horizon/turnover typology. Closeness to D: ADJACENT (holdings overlap network), no horizon dimension.

title: Birds of a Feather: Do Hedge Fund Managers Flock Together?
summary: Gerritzen, Jackwerth, Plazzi (Management Science 70(5) 2024, 2976-2998; IDEAS abstract). Outcome: pairwise similarity of hedge funds' investing (distance of returns; holdings similarity) for UK hedge funds; peer/tie = shared prior employer and overlapping tenure (managerial ties), 2002-2013 FCA filings; joint effect accounts for up to two thirds of difference in investing behavior; pairwise dyad regressions. Closeness to A: PARTIAL-ADJACENT (tie-induced convergence of hedge-fund investing behavior, via returns/holdings, not turnover or horizon); to D: not horizon-based similarity.

title: Birds of a Feather : Do Hedge Fund Managers Flock Together?
summary: Konstanz KOPS record of Gerritzen-Jackwerth-Plazzi 'Birds of a Feather' (WP). Duplicate/companion of the Management Science abstract; see birds-of-a-feather-do-hedge-fund-managers-flock-together. Notes 2016 WP listing said joint effect about a fifth, published version up to two thirds.

title: Brian Bushee
summary: Bushee's data page for the public transient/quasi-indexer/dedicated institutional investor classification (1981-2025, updated July 2026); requires Thomson Reuters 13F merge; also type, style, growth and tax-sensitivity classifications.

title: Calibrating emergent phenomena in stock markets with agent based models - PMC
summary: PLOS ONE 2018 'Calibrating emergent phenomena in stock markets with agent-based models' (PMC5834198): two-agent models with heterogeneous investment horizons, decision processes (minority/majority games) and decision lags calibrated to index series; states horizon heterogeneity is crucial for reproducing long memory in ABMs; anomalous predictability precedes dotcom/GFC. Calibrates horizons to index price series, not holdings; no network or neighbour-driven horizon adaptation.

title: CFR Working Paper NO. 15-06
Common Ownership in America: 1980–2017
summary: Backus-Conlon-Sinkinson (AEJ Micro 2021/NBER 25454): scraped all 13(f) filings 1999-2017 (318,038 filings, 25GB) because Thomson s34 has gaps and errors; XML-era reliability from mid-2013. Data-quality evidence for 13F-based work.

title: CoMSES Catalog
summary: Li, Nishimura & Men (2014, Physica A) ABM built on the Fractal Market Hypothesis: agents with different investment horizons; liquidity supplied across horizons; market gains stability as structure moves from uniformity to diversification, but with finite maximum horizon more diversity does not necessarily bring more stability (greater fluctuation on large time scales). No network structure, no homophily, no horizon adaptation, no empirical holdings calibration (authors note real data cannot identify investor horizons). Closest published FMH-ABM to the paper's horizon-diversity-stability claim; supports opposite-sign-friction-channel discussion.

title: CoMSES Catalog
summary: Li, Li & Sun (2017, Applied Economics) FMH-based ABM: greater divergence of investors' horizons makes market more stable, efficient, less crash-prone; interactions and herding cause crashes when the divergent structure shrinks to limited horizons; heterogeneous horizons provide liquidity; explains momentum (short-term)/contrarian (long-term). Herding present but not network-structured horizon similarity; no endogenous horizon adaptation to neighbours; no empirical calibration. Directly prior art for 'horizon diversity compression -> fragility' (paper's temporal echo chamber outcome).

title: Crash Risk and Investor Horizon
summary: Zhu (Calgary WP, 1981-2008 CRSP/13F; later version appears as HAL post-print 'Investor heterogeneity and negative skewness in stock returns', JIFMIM 2022, doi 10.1016/j.intfin.2022.101690). Quarterly return skewness (and alternatives) regressed on LEVELS of short-term (top tertile of 4-qtr average Yan-Zhang churn rate) vs long-term (bottom tertile) institutional ownership; negative IO-skewness link (Aggarwal-Rao 1990) is driven by short-term IO; long-term IO and trading positively related to skewness; short-term IO also linked to corporate risk-taking. Churn rate = min(buy,sell)/avg portfolio value, where buys/sells are computed as |N_t P_t - N_{t-1} P_{t-1} - N_{t-1} dP_t| i.e. ALREADY corrects for price drift. Design is level-of-short-horizon-ownership only; no dispersion or heterogeneity-within-stock measure. Closest prior art for crash-risk-by-horizon (pivot B level-effects baseline).

title: Crowded spaces and anomalies
summary: IMPORTANT NAMING CORRECTION: the 'Ludwig' crowding paper is by Ludwig (first name) Chincarini, Renato Lazo-Paz and Fabio Moneta; AEA/EFMA 2022 draft 'Following the crowd: Anomalies and crowding by Institutional Investors' became 'Crowded spaces and anomalies', Journal of Banking & Finance 182 (Jan 2026), 107579 (SSRN 4618248). RePEc abstract only. Uses 13F holdings and a Days-ADV crowding measure (days institutions would need to liquidate; from secondary summaries, unverified). Finds anomaly returns concentrated in the most crowded long-leg / least crowded short-leg stocks, persisting post-publication, and hypothesises crowding raises institutions' crash-risk exposure. Crowding here is LEVEL of same-stock ownership overlap, not horizon or horizon dispersion; no investor-horizon conditioning. Closest adjacent work to pivot B only via the crowding-crash channel; does not test heterogeneity of holder horizons. JBF IF about 3-4, a plausible venue benchmark.

title: Do global financial crises validate assertions of fractal market hypothesis? | International Economics and Economic Policy | Springer Nature Link
summary: Springer abstract only (paywalled): Int. Economics and Economic Policy 14:153-165 (2017; online Nov 2015). Replicates Kristoufek (2013) wavelet-power test across global stock markets and multiple crises; reports dominance of higher frequencies during crises, claimed robust across countries and crises. Same index-return, frequency-domain design; no investor-level horizon data. Authors not captured in the fetch; full text not read, so treat numbers as unverified.

title: Do Institutional Investors Prefer Nearâ€ Term Earnings over Longâ€ Run Value?
summary: IDEAS/RePEc abstract of Bushee 2001 CAR 18(2): transient ownership linked to near-term earnings weighting and myopic pricing with abnormal-return trading strategy; banks show none. Abstract only (full text not obtained; SSRN 161739 bot-blocked).

title: Do Institutional Investors Stabilize
summary: Glossner, Matos, Ramelli, Wagner (ECGI WP 688/2020 rev Jan 2025; CEPR DP15070; Management Science 2025 per ECGI listing). COVID-19 crash Q1-2020: stocks with higher pre-crisis IO (Q4-2019) performed worse, unrelated to analyst earnings revisions; effect mitigated by LONG-TERM (Gaspar-Massa-Matos 2005 classification), passive (BlackRock/Vanguard/State St) and foreign IO. Mechanisms: downscaling (redemptions, quick reversal) vs repositioning toward financially resilient firms (persistent); hedge funds sell indiscriminately; retail (Vanda Research, Robinhood) provide liquidity. Mean passive IO 16%, long-term IO 37%. Horizon enters as LEVEL (share of IO held by long-term investors); no dispersion of holder horizons within a stock and no test of whether long-horizon holders absorb short-horizon selling in the same stock. Direct evidence for pivot B's stress-episode setting: levels only, retail is the identified liquidity provider.

title: Do Peer Firms Aﬀect Corporate Financial Policy?∗
summary: Leary & Roberts (JF 2014; Berkeley working-paper draft) 'Do Peer Firms Affect Corporate Financial Policy?'. Finance template for peer-effect identification under Manski's reflection problem: instrument peer firms' financial policy with peers' IDIOSYNCRATIC stock return shocks (relevance via return-financing link; exclusion by controlling for own return and industry return and showing shocks are serially uncorrelated and cross-uncorrelated), with a customer-industry placebo (Cohen-Frazzini logic). Finding: one-s.d. change in peers' leverage -> ~11% change in own leverage; mimicking strongest in small, constrained firms with less experienced CEOs; peer characteristics other than return shocks largely irrelevant. Analogue for horizon contagion: use exogenous shocks to neighbours (flow shocks, index-reconstitution, idiosyncratic return shocks on non-co-held stocks) as instruments.

title: Does Common Ownership Really Increase Firm Coordination?
summary: Lewellen-Lowry (JFE 141:322-344, 2021) via Harvard Forum summary. Reviews four identification approaches (financial-institution mergers, S&P 500 entry, Russell reconstitution). Merger sample has 60+ events over decades but the treated-firm list is dominated by one event, BlackRock-BGI 2009, coinciding with post-crisis response; treated sample tilted to growth firms, so DiD produces spurious 'treatment' effects; once modified to account for this, no evidence mergers changed firm decisions. Russell reconstitutions do not move institution-level common ownership enough. Implication for pivot A shock design: merger shocks are timing-confounded by dominant events and style/characteristic exposure; need style x quarter FE, event-clustering, many-merger pooled design, drop BlackRock-BGI robustness, and pre-trend tests.

title: Does communication increase investors’ trading frequency? Evidence from a Chinese social trading platform | Financial Innovation | Springer Nature Link
summary: Jin and Yu (Financial Innovation 2022) 'Does communication increase investors trading frequency? Evidence from a Chinese social trading platform'. Outcome: individual investors' trading frequency; peer = communication on social trading platform; retail only. Closeness to A: ADJACENT (peer communication and trading frequency, retail platform, not institutional, no portfolio-overlap peers).

title: Does herding behavior reveal skill?
summary: Jiang and Verardo (JF forthcoming 2017/2018): fund-level dynamic herding measure (tendency to follow institutional crowd's trades); herding funds underperform antiherding by >2%/yr, gap persistent, attributed to skill and career concerns. Outcome: fund alpha. Turnover appears only as a CONTROL and as a determinant: herding funds are older and less active (LOWER portfolio turnover) in Table 3 cross-sectional regression of herding on size, age, expense, turnover, flows, alpha. Not about peer influence on horizon; herding measured vs aggregate crowd, not neighbours. Relevance: shows herding propensity correlates negatively with turnover (fund trait), a fact pivot A must separate from peer convergence.

title: DOI: 10.16538/j.cnki.fem.20260118.204
summary: Chen Kai, Lu Rong, Qin Shan, Foreign Economics & Management 48(5), 2026 (Chinese; received 2024-07). Stock-level institutional TRADING-HORIZON HOMOGENEITY (THomo = -log CV of holders' half-yearly churn rates, per Chan-Cheng-Hameed 2022 CV; AvgCR/StdCR across a stock's institutional holders) raises left-tail systemic risk (SJC copula tail dependence), via liquidity-shock and order-imbalance channels; stronger under policy uncertainty, weak markets, arbitrage risk. This is a near-duplicate of Pivot B (holder-horizon dispersion as fragility predictor) in A-shares. Direction consistent with the user's stock-level slope (less dispersion, more risk). Overturns the 'no direct prior art for dispersion and crash/tail risk' claim (cc-5) for China; US evidence still open.

title: DP12021 Adapting to Radical Change: The Benefits of Short-Horizon Investors | CEPR
summary: CEPR DP12021 abstract page for Giannetti & Yu, 'Adapting to Radical Change: The Benefits of Short-Horizon Investors' (Management Science 67(7):4032-4055, 2021; the batch DOI 10.1093/rfs/hhaa070 does not match - the paper is in Management Science, DOI 10.1287/mnsc.2020.3702). Firms with more short-term institutional owners suffer smaller sales/investment/employment drops after permanent negative competitive shocks (tariff cuts, deregulation) via R&D, differentiation, executive turnover. Abstract only; corporate outcomes, off-axis for pivots; shows short-horizon investors are not uniformly harmful.

title: DP15070 Do institutional investors stabilize equity markets in crisis periods? Evidence from COVID-19 | CEPR
Econometrics of Network Models
summary: de Paula (2017) 'Econometrics of Network Models' (Advances in Economics and Econometrics, 11th World Congress ch. 8; CeMMAP WP). Survey of identification in linear-in-means network models, games on networks, and network formation; covers Manski reflection problem, Bramoulle et al. intransitivity conditions, correlated effects/endogenous network formation, and identification with partially observed networks. Reference for endogenous-network and measurement-of-network concerns.

title: ECONOMETRICS OF SAMPLED NETWORKS
summary: Chandrasekhar & Lewis (working paper; Stanford) 'Econometrics of Sampled Networks'. Network-statistics and regressions on sampled networks suffer errors-in-variables bias even if full-network identification holds; Proposition 3.4: 2SLS using sampled-graph-based friends-of-friends instruments generically yields E[Z u] != 0 (invalid) when the sampled network omits nodes (peer l unobserved makes x_k enter y_i via y_l). Offers analytic corrections and a graphical-reconstruction approach. Relevance: if peers are restricted to the top-150 filers (a sample of the 13F universe) or neighbours constructed from a subset of stocks, instruments built from the observed graph are invalid.

title: EconPapers: Does common ownership really increase firm coordination?
summary: RePEc abstract for Lewellen-Lowry JFE 2021: effects attributed to common ownership caused by other factors (differential responses to 2008 crisis); propose modified approach less sensitive; little robust evidence common ownership affects firm behavior. Full text not retrievable (SSRN/ECGI/JFE fetch returned JUNK_CONTENT); use Harvard Forum note for mechanics.

title: EconPapers: EVOLUTION AND TIME HORIZONS IN AN AGENT-BASED STOCK MARKET
summary: LeBaron (2001, Macroeconomic Dynamics 5:225-254) ABM where agents differ in lookback horizon used to evaluate forecasting rules; evolution via wealth-based replacement of poor agents by new draws, so horizon distribution evolves endogenously. Results: replicates REE with long-horizon agents, but evolving mixed population to long horizons alone is difficult; mixed short/long populations raise return variability and give volatility/volume patterns like real markets. Endogenous horizon evolution already exists (performance/wealth-based selection), but NO network, NO neighbour-based adaptation, NO homophily, NO empirical calibration. Key prior art for pivot E.

title: EconPapers: Evolution and Time Horizons in an Agent-Based Stock Market
summary: CEF 1999 working-paper version of LeBaron (2001) 'Evolution and Time Horizons in an Agent-Based Stock Market': single risky stock, stochastic dividend, agents choose among rules via performance memory length (horizon); wealth-weighted price impact and evolutionary replacement of poor agents. Duplicate/early version of the Macro Dynamics paper.

title: EconPapers: Institutional investor network and idiosyncratic volatility of stocks
summary: Zhai et al., Economics & Politics 36(3) 2024: institutional investor network built from heavy co-holdings in China; density negatively and centrality positively related to idiosyncratic volatility. Network-of-co-holding to volatility prior art; no horizon dimension.

title: EconPapers: Understanding How Short-Termism and a Dynamic Investor Network Affects Investor Returns: An Agent-Based Perspective
summary: Oldham (Complexity 2019, 1715624) ABM: investors with different time horizons, advisor network that evolves by connecting to outperforming investors; finding: short-term behaviour raises volatility; neighbour-following affects network effects. Closest published ABM analogue of the current paper's model: horizon heterogeneity plus dynamic network, but link formation is performance-based not horizon-homophilous, no empirical 13F calibration. Closeness to pivot E / model: PARTIAL; to A/D empirics: none.

title: EconPapers: Who Is Afraid of BlackRock?
summary: Massa-Schumacher-Wang RFS 34(4):1987-2044 (2021), abstract. BlackRock-BGI merger and a large global sample of asset-management mergers: open-end funds with large exposure to commonly held stocks AVOID those stocks after announcement; permanent change in institutional ownership composition, negative price and liquidity impact; 'market participants behave strategically in response to changes in expected financial fragility.' KEY for pivot A: merger shocks directly change neighbours' trading/holdings via an anticipated-fragility channel, so a merger violates the exclusion restriction for a horizon-contagion test (neighbours respond to concentration, not to merging party's horizon). Also precedent that merger designs on fund trading behaviour exist (Connected stocks).

title: Electronic copy available at: http://ssrn.com/abstract=1464954
summary: Cremers & Pareek (Yale ICF WP 09-19, Aug 2009) 'Institutional Investors' Investment Durations and Stock Return Anomalies' (early version of what became JFE/RFS-line duration work). Introduces stock-level 'average stock duration' = amount-weighted average of the length of time each holder has held the stock (look-back to date of initial purchase), plus residual duration orthogonalized to turnover. Shows momentum, reversal, accruals, share issuance anomalies stronger where short-duration institutions hold more; duration predicts next-quarter idiosyncratic volatility (overconfidence story à la DHS). Alternative 13F horizon measures: turnover, Bushee transient share. Duration is a holding-period (survival) measure, not a flow ratio, so it is immune to value-weight price drift. Level of short-term ownership only; no dispersion of holder horizons.

title: Electronic copy available at: http://ssrn.com/abstract=2498743
summary: Cremers & Pareek (JFE 2016, author draft Dec 2015) 'Patient capital outperformance'. Fund Duration = time the fund has held $1 of equities over previous five years; high Active Share + duration >2 years outperform ~2.3%/yr (2.22% institutions); retail-fund median holding duration 14 months; top-quintile patient+active institutions hold ~2.1% of assets. Another duration-based horizon (survival measure, no price-drift issue). Level, not dispersion; fund-level performance, not market stability.

title: Empirical Challenges with Peers-of-Peers Instruments
summary: Canen & Chadha (arXiv 2602.24215 v2, Jul 2026) 'Empirical Challenges with Peers-of-Peers Instruments in the Linear-In-Means Model'. Using random graph theory they show friends-of-friends instruments degenerate in very sparse networks and carry too little first-stage information in denser networks, so IVs may be weak or the first-stage estimand undefined; adapt Anderson-Rubin weak-IV-robust inference; row-scaling the adjacency matrix can mitigate. Revisits empirical applications showing the issue is prevalent. Directly on point for A: a dense portfolio-overlap network among institutions means G^2 x instruments are weak; report AR confidence sets and first-stage F, and consider alternative instruments (exogenous shocks, non-overlap neighbours).

title: ERASMUS UNIVERSITY ROTTERDAM
summary: Master thesis (Erasmus Rotterdam, Aug 2021, Escobar; supervisor Gryglewicz). Dutch pension funds and insurers 2007-early 2021: life insurers countercyclical independent of regime; pension funds and non-life insurers procyclical in normal times; only insurers support markets in stress incl COVID-19. LOW authority (student thesis); bond/asset class aggregate, no horizon measure. Gray-lit corroboration of Timmer sign.

title: Escobar and Pedraza 2023 JFE: Active trading and (poor) performance: the social transmission channel
summary: Quasi-random classroom assignment of new retail investors: exposure to peers with positive outcomes raises own start of trading, trading frequency, speculative trading, lower profits. Retail-only; best identification precedent (random peer assignment) for peer effects in trading frequency/holding period, but no institutional sample. Abstract-level from search relay.

title: Executive Compensation and Short-Termism∗
summary: Piccolo (Oxford, 2018 draft). Model where inefficient corporate short-termism is a self-fulfilling prophecy via strategic complementarities between firm investment horizon and investors' choice of whether to acquire information on short-term performance or long-term value; severity of manager agency problem determines equilibrium. Firm-side, not investor-network; but supplies a formal template for horizon complementarity (multiple equilibria in horizon-linked info acquisition).

title: Facebook Finance: How Social Interaction Propagates Active Investing
summary: Heimer and Simon (FRB Cleveland WP 15-22, 2015) 'Facebook Finance'. Outcome: retail traders' trading activity; peer definition: contacts on a social trading network (eToro-type FX platform); good short-term performance triggers contact; activity rises when peers perform well and communicate; identification: staggered brokerage entry into partnership with the social platform. Retail FX traders, individual-level trading records. Closeness to A: ADJACENT (peer effects in trading activity with causal ID), retail not institutional, activity not horizon/holding period, no portfolio-overlap network.

title: Finance and Economics Discussion Series
Finance Research Letters | Journal | ScienceDirect.com by Elsevier
summary: Elsevier journal homepage (fetched 2026-11-18): Impact Factor 7.1, CiteScore 10.1, APC USD 3,540. Scope: all areas of finance, desk review by Editors-in-Chief, papers <2,500 words, topics list includes Contagion/crises/interdependence, Financial Mathematics and Econophysics, Behavioral finance, Microstructure. Fits both 13F network empirics and ABMs (econophysics explicitly listed) but letter format limits depth; IF is above 4-5 threshold.

title: Financial instability transition under heterogeneous investments and
summary: Forera, Budnick, Vivo, Aufiero, Bartolucci, Caccioli (arXiv 2501.19260, Jan 2025) 'Financial instability transition under heterogeneous investments and portfolio diversification'. Random-matrix dynamical model of financial institutions with overlapping portfolios driven by portfolio rebalancing; heterogeneity of investments generally correlates with higher volatility; diversification can stabilize or destabilize depending on connectivity; stability governed by largest eigenvalue. Relevance: a 2025 physics-style model where heterogeneity of investment strategy interacts with overlap-network connectivity to set market stability, directly relevant to novelty of model-based pivot E (heterogeneity vs stability), but heterogeneity is in portfolio composition, not lookback horizon; no empirical calibration to 13F.

title: Fractal Markets Hypothesis and the Global Financial Crisis:
summary: Kristoufek (2012/13, arXiv 1203.4979) tests Fractal Markets Hypothesis predictions on DJI, NASDAQ, S&P500 around the GFC, using novel scaling-of-variance measures of trading activity at different investment horizons. Finds FMH predictions (loss of horizon diversity/ liquidity in crises, dominance of short horizons) fit observed behaviour well. Purely time-series on index returns; no holdings data, no network, no agent-level horizon adaptation. Useful as the empirical FMH benchmark: horizon structure inferred from return scaling, not from investor holdings.

title: Fractal Markets Hypothesis and the Global Financial Crisis: Wavelet Power Evidence - PMC
summary: Kristoufek (Sci Rep 3:2857, 2013; PMC full text) tests the FMH prediction that turbulent periods are dominated by a narrow set of (short) investment horizons, using continuous wavelet power spectra as scale-specific variance on major indices (NASDAQ, FTSE, CAC, DAX, HSI, Nikkei) around the 2000 dot-com bust, 2008 Lehman collapse and 2011-12 Eurozone crisis, with red-noise significance tests. Finds high-frequency (short-horizon) dominance in the most turbulent GFC windows, consistent with FMH. Limits for our audit: horizon structure is inferred purely from index-return variance across scales, not from investor holdings; no agent-level horizon, no network, no causal test of withdrawal of long-horizon investors. Complements the arXiv 1203.4979 scaling-of-variance paper already in vault (same author, different method).

title: Gradual information diffusion across commonly owned firms
summary: Ying (JFE 156, 2024, 103852) abstract/IDEAS page only (full text restricted; no open copy found; SSRN/author copy not located). Outcome: cross-predictability of monthly stock returns among commonly owned firms (CIO-based peer momentum); peers = firms linked by common institutional owners. Mechanism concentrated in institutions with few holdings, passive, low portfolio turnover. Uses turnover only as a mechanism descriptor of the owners, not as an outcome. Closeness to A: NONE (stock-level information diffusion, not investor horizon convergence); to D: adjacent (co-ownership network, low-turnover owners drive effect) but no horizon-similarity test.

title: Herd on the Street: Informational Inefficiencies in a Market with Short-Term Speculation | NBER
summary: Froot-Scharfstein-Stein NBER WP 3250 (1990), JF 47:1461-1484 (1992). Abstract: if speculators have short horizons they may herd on the same information, trying to learn what other informed traders know; multiple herding equilibria; they may study information unrelated to fundamentals; equilibria informationally inefficient. KEY theory for horizon spreading: short horizon makes value of information depend on what OTHERS trade on -> strategic complementarity of short horizons (a short-horizon trader's best response is more short-horizon when others are). Gives pivot A a sign: positive peer effect in horizon via complementarity; also predicts multiple equilibria (tipping), not smooth diffusion. Caveat: horizon is exogenous in FSS; endogenous horizon choice is an extension. Abstract-only (NBER page).

title: Herding, Momentum, and Reversal in China’s A-Share Market: An Agent-Based
summary: arXiv 2607.27063 (2026): network ABM for China A-shares separating belief updating from social imitation; action probabilities shift toward neighbours' recent actions; Watts-Strogatz rewiring is random. No horizon state, no horizon homophily, imitation weight not tied to a holdings-based peer coefficient.

title: Herding, Momentum, and Reversal in China’s A-Share Market: An Agent-Based Network Model with Information Diffusion
summary: Weng (arXiv 2607.27063, Jul 2026): ABM on lattices/ER/Watts-Strogatz networks where investors shift buy/sell/hold probabilities toward neighbours' recent actions, with separate information diffusion; compares CSAD/LSV with tail-based herding indicator on China A-shares. Network imitation of ACTIONS, not horizons; no homophily rule; no horizon variable; no holdings data. Illustrates that network ABMs imitate actions/opinions.

title: Heterogeneity of institutional ownership and stock price delay
summary: Chen, Lee, Sun WP (2015; 13F 1981Q1-2013Q4). Stock price delay (Hou-Moskowitz) regressed on ownership shares of institution TYPES defined from the institution's perspective: low/high churn rate (bottom/top tertile of 4-qtr avg Yan-Zhang churn rate), concentrated (top-tercile HHI), skilled, independent; and from stock's perspective (top-5, year-long holders). Finding: low-churn and top-5 ownership lower price delay; high-churn, concentrated, skilled ownership raise it; delay components of concentrated/skilled holders priced. Churn rate formula nets out price change (N_{t-1}*dP) i.e. share-based, drift-corrected. Heterogeneity = share of ownership by type buckets, NOT a within-stock dispersion (SD/entropy) of holders' horizons. Relevant to (c) as the nearest 'ownership composition' design and to (f) as an example of drift-corrected churn.

title: Heterogeneous Agent Models in Economics and Finance
summary: IDEAS/RePEc listing page for Hommes (2006) Handbook of Computational Economics chapter 23; metadata duplicate of the TI working paper note ti-2005-0561.

summary: LeBaron (2010/2011 Brandeis WP10R) heterogeneous gain (memory length) learning ABM: agents weight past differently in return and volatility forecasting; wealth-weighted evolution; produces long swings in prices from fundamentals; agents with heavy weight on recent past control large wealth share and perpetuate volatility-magnifying dynamics. Memory/horizon heterogeneity with evolutionary adaptation again; no network, no homophily, no holdings calibration (calibrated only to dividend/price series moments).

summary: Golub & Jackson (QJE 2012, 127(3):1287-1338; Stanford working-paper Nov 2011 version). Theory: with DeGroot-style averaging of neighbours' beliefs/behaviours, convergence to consensus is SLOWED by homophily (group-biased interaction frequencies; a new homophily measure based on relative interaction frequencies) but is not affected by network density; in contrast, viral spread along shortest paths speeds with density and is independent of homophily. Key theoretical backbone for the current paper's 'temporal echo chamber' mechanism: homophily plus averaging adaptation (horizon adapting toward neighbours' horizons) implies slow cross-group convergence, and within-group fast convergence. Not about investors; zero horizon content. Cite as the formal justification for the horizon-adaptation-with-homophily model; also provides the spectral/second-eigenvalue convergence-time tool that could give an analytic (not just simulated) adaptation-speed result.

title: Identiﬁcation of Endogenous Social Eﬀects: The
summary: NOT the Manski 1993 paper: lecture slides (Japanese seminar, 2013) summarizing Manski (1993, REStud 60:531-542): endogenous vs exogenous (contextual) vs correlated effects; linear-in-means reflection problem (perfect collinearity of E[y|x] with E[z|x] and x); tautological beta=1 if reference group defined by x; dynamic lag-timing assumption; nonlinear models. Secondary, low authority; original publisher PDF bot-blocked (Cloudflare) and free copies (scispace, AgEcon) returned HTTP 202.

title: Impact of different investment horizons in heterogeneous agent models: Do long-term traders bring market stability?
summary: Impact of different investment horizons in heterogeneous agent models: do long-term traders bring market stability? JEBO 196 (2022) 393-401. Brock-Hommes switching model with horizons; longer horizon reduces the fraction adopting the strategy; stability effect. Prior art for pivot E (ABM with horizon heterogeneity) but no network adaptation / empirical calibration.

title: Inferring latent social networks from stock holdings
summary: Hong and Xu (JFE 131(2) 2019, 323-344): infer latent investor social networks from holdings; manager linkages to a city overdispersed vs Erdos-Renyi; non-iid managers have more alumni in that city and outperform there. Method precedent for inferring networks from 13F-type holdings (homophily/network inference, topic g). No horizon/turnover outcome.

summary: Izadifar-Rahmati arXiv 2607.12067 (2026): graph ML (dynamic node affinities) forecasting 13F institutional holdings. Methodological; not about horizons; shows 13F dynamic-graph modelling crowding.

title: Institutional Herding
summary: Sias (RFS 17(1) 2004, 165-206; IDEAS abstract). Institutional demand this quarter correlates with lag institutional demand (13F quarterly); herding = following each other plus own lag trades; little due to momentum; consistent with inferring information from each other's trades. Outcome: cross-sectional correlation of institutional demand (fraction of institutions buying). Not horizon/turnover. NOTE: assigned DOI 10.1093/rfs/hhg036 is not this paper per RePEc (Sias is hhg035); hhg036 could not be fetched (Cloudflare) so identity unverified.

title: Institutional Investment Horizon
summary: Doering, Drobetz, El Ghoul, Guedhami, Schroeder (EFMA 2019), 'Institutional Investment Horizon and Firm Valuation: A Global Perspective', 34 countries. Horizon via Gaspar-Massa-Matos churn ratio; short-horizon institutions drive the positive institutional-ownership/firm-value link, more so with liquid markets (exit-threat discipline). Useful for (b): confirms the churn-ratio horizon convention is standard (and reviews its lineage: Gaspar-Massa-Matos 2005, Yan-Zhang 2009, Cremers-Pareek, Harford-Kecskes-Mansi 2018), and shows horizon-level effects are the entire literature; no dispersion, network or peer concept.

title: Institutional Investor Classification Data:  Variable Definitions – Brian Bushee
summary: Bushee's variable definitions for TRA/QIX/DED classification: annual averages of four 13F reports, momentum variables dropped after Bushee 1998, factor-score extension, modal permanent classification (first-order autocorrelation about 0.8), recycled Spectrum manager numbers and unreliable type codes after 1998; accuracy not guaranteed. Authoritative methodology page (author source).

title: Institutional Investor Cliques and Governance
summary: Crane, Koch, Michaely (Drexel/Harvard Corp Gov Forum 2016; RFS-style WP) institutional investor CLIQUES in ownership network: about 20 cliques per year; institutions in cliques most likely dedicated (Bushee 1998), least likely quasi-indexers; clique ownership affects governance/voting. Closeness to D: PARTIAL-ADJACENT (institution-type, i.e. Bushee-type, composition of co-holding cliques, a form of type clustering in co-holding), but not a horizon-proximity vs portfolio-similarity correlation; outcome is governance.

title: Institutional Investor Diversity, Herding Behavior, and Systemic Financial Risk: Evidence from China
summary: Zhang-Miao-Zhang, Risks 13(12):243 (Dec 2025; MDPI, low-tier). 'Institutional investor diversity' index (CV + entropy-weight over investment scale, experience, concentration; NOT horizon) across 84 Chinese listed financial institutions 2016-2024; greater diversity lowers EVT-based systemic risk via less herding. Adjacent evidence that investor-base diversity (not level) matters, but not horizon, not crash risk of individual stocks, not skewness.

summary: Elsaify (Duke dissertation 2021) heterogeneous institutional investors, capability/factor timing; hedge funds most capable, insurers/pensions least. Low relevance to horizon-dispersion pivot.

title: Institutional Investors and Equity Returns:
summary: Yan & Zhang (RFS 2009) 'Institutional investors and equity returns: are short-term institutions better informed?' (Lehigh author copy). Churn rate (Gaspar-style, numerator |S_t P_t - S_{t-1}P_{t-1} - S_{t-1}(P_t-P_{t-1})|, MIN of buys and sells over average value, 4-quarter average) to classify short- vs long-term institutions; short-term institutional ownership subsumes the predictive power of total IO for returns; short-term institutions' trades forecast returns and earnings surprises, no long-run reversal. Min(buy,sell) specifically removes investor cash flows. Confirms price-drift-adjusted numerator is standard in the literature (pivot C prior art); LEVEL of short-term ownership only.

summary: Duarte & Parsa (MIT WP Apr 2011) intrinsic trading frequency (institution fixed-effect turnover) as horizon proxy; stocks with lowest-trading-frequency holders earn ~6pp/yr higher returns than highest. Level of holder horizon -> returns; no dispersion or stress test. Useful for measurement: shows institution-fixed-effect horizon proxy to remove time-varying contamination.

summary: Fan-Fu, Emerging Markets Review 42 (2020). China A-shares: institutional ownership LEVEL raises crash risk via selling pressure after bad news; stronger for transient, weaker for dedicated (Bushee); institutional competition amplifies it. Level/type only; no dispersion of horizons.

Investor Heterogeneity and Liquidity*
summary: Chan, Cheng, Hameed (JFQA 57(7):2798-2833, 2022; WP Feb 2021). CLOSEST PAPER TO PIVOT B (dispersion half). Horizon measure: Gaspar-Massa-Matos churn rate per institution-quarter from 13F; STDCR = cross-holder SD of churn among a stock's institutional holders / mean churn (unscaled USTDCR also shown). This is a DISPERSION (not level) measure, controls for IO level, concentration, number of institutions. Outcomes: Amihud illiquidity, inverse turnover, and their volatility (CV). Sign: more heterogeneous horizons -> more liquid, lower liquidity volatility (1 SD STDCR lowers illiquidity ~0.7% full sample, 1.9% (LOGILLIQ) to 7.4% (1/TURN) in 2000-2016; low-vs-high quintile illiquidity differs 63%/37%). Mechanism: same-horizon funds have correlated flows (fund-flow comovement higher within same churn tercile, Table 2), so homogeneous investor base = correlated liquidity demand; heterogeneous base lets long-horizon funds provide liquidity to fire-selling short-horizon funds. Identification: 2003 dividend tax reform shock to investor heterogeneity; extreme flow-induced trading (Coval-Stafford) has larger price impact and reversal when STDCR low; illiquidity premium concentrated in low-heterogeneity stocks. Sample CRSP/Thomson 13F ~1980-2016, US. NOT tested: volatility/crash/fragility as outcomes, stress-episode within-stock absorption by horizon type, Bushee entropy, share-based vs value-weight contamination (churn uses value-based |N_t P_t - N_{t-1}P_{t-1}| per Gaspar et al unless otherwise noted). Verdict: pivot B's dispersion-to-liquidity piece is PRE-EMPTED; residual novelty = volatility/crash/price-delay outcomes, stress episodes, contamination-free (share-based) measure, ownership-weighted dispersion, within-stock panel.

title: Investor Horizons and Corporate Policies
summary: Harvard Corporate Governance Forum post (13 Feb 2013) summarizing Derrien, Kecskes, Thesmar, 'Investor Horizons and Corporate Policies' (JFQA). NOTE: authors are Derrien-Kecskes-Thesmar, not Harford-Kecskes-Mansi as the batch label said. Finds long-horizon ownership raises investment/equity issuance and lowers payouts when firms are undervalued; supports 'catering' over 'capital-structure arbitrage'. Corporate-policy outcomes only; secondary/blog-level provenance. Peripheral to pivots A-E (shows level of long-term ownership matters conditionally, no dispersion, no peer effects).

title: Investors' horizon and stock prices
summary: Parsa (MIT PhD thesis 2011, advisors Angeletos & Lorenzoni) 'Investors' horizon and stock prices'. Ch.1 model: short-horizon informed traders raise price noise (negative informational externality on long-term investors). Ch.2 constructs 'intrinsic trading frequency' = 13F institution fixed effect in trading frequency after controlling for market/portfolio characteristics (1980-2005); stocks held by high-frequency investors have higher volatility, driven by cash-flow component; low-frequency-held prices forecast long-run returns. Ch.3 (with Fernando Duarte): lowest-quintile-frequency stocks earn ~6pp/yr more than highest-quintile, robust to FF/liquidity/momentum. Establishes institution fixed-effect view of horizon (persistence) -> investor horizon is a stable trait, which cuts against peer-driven adaptation (pivot A) unless within-institution variation is identified. Ownership-weighted level only; no dispersion, no networks.

title: Investors' Horizons and the Amplification of Market Shocks
summary: Cella, Ellul, Giannetti (June 2010 draft; RFS 2013) 'Investors' Horizons and the Amplification of Market Shocks'. Horizon = churn ratio (Gaspar et al. 2005), 1990-2006, mean 0.34 / median 0.22, stable across time (treated as permanent trait). Lehman Sept 2008 shock: short-term institutions sold ~21% of portfolios vs ~7% for long-term; stocks with high 'investor turnover' (ownership-weighted churn) fell more and reversed more; high-IT stocks have higher volatility. Fig. 4: short-term investors sell similar fractions of high- and low-IT stocks, so selling is a trader trait not a stock trait. Closest existing evidence for pivot B (horizon and fragility in stress) but ownership-weighted LEVEL only; does not test dispersion of holder horizons nor whether long-horizon holders in the same stock absorb short-horizon selling (they report modest inflows in short-term-held stocks). Remains the key benchmark for any 'stress episode' extension.

title: ISSN 0956-8549-717
summary: Cella, Ellul, Giannetti, FMG Discussion Paper 717 (longer/later version of the Investors' Horizons and Amplification of Market Shocks paper). Same churn-ratio measure and Lehman shock design; duplicate-family of the NY Fed 2010 draft.

title: ISSN 0956-8549-717
summary: Cella, Ellul, Giannetti, 'Investors' Horizons and the Amplification of Market Shocks' (LSE FMG DP717 Feb 2013; RFS 26(7):1607-1648). Short-horizon institutions (churn ratio, average of lagged quarters; predetermined) sell more during turmoil (VIX-defined episodes, e.g. 2008, 2001, etc.) and sales are not just withdrawals; stocks with more short-horizon holders show larger price drops and reversals (fire-sale amplification). Identification: instrument for turnover using correlation of investor past performance with withdrawals. Directly relevant to pivot B: it is the LEVEL-of-short-horizon-ownership baseline; shows short horizons demand liquidity in stress - the 'long-horizon absorb short-horizon selling' idea is the mirror image and is partially addressed there (they discuss reduced buy-side capital), so pivot B must be framed on dispersion of holder horizons and within-stock absorption flows, not level. Cited by the user's Section on (b).

title: IZA DP No. 2652
summary: Bramoulle, Djebbari, Fortin (IZA DP 2652, Mar 2007; J. Econometrics 150(1) 2009 41-55) 'Identification of Peer Effects through Social Networks' (working paper version of the assigned DOI paper; publisher page was bot-blocked). Extends Manski linear-in-means to agent-specific reference groups on a network. Endogenous and contextual effects are generally identified (reflection problem solved) under intransitivity: if some peers of peers are not peers, G^2 x (peers-of-peers characteristics) instruments for peers' mean outcome Gy. Necessary and sufficient rank conditions (I, G, G^2 linearly independent); assumes correlated unobservables absent or component fixed effects; fails for some structures (e.g., complete bipartite, complete graphs). Monte Carlo: density and intransitivity matter for precision. Referee relevance: portfolio-overlap networks among 150 large institutions are dense and highly transitive (top holdings overlap), so G^2 instruments are weak/invalid; Angrist/Canen-Chadha challenges apply.

Positions itself relative to the investor-horizon literature (Derrien-Kecskes-Thesmar 2013; Cella-Ellul-Giannetti 2013) as a 'new perspective on investor composition risk'. title: Journal of Financial Economics 76 (2005) 135–165
summary: Gaspar, Massa, Matos (JFE 2005) 'Shareholder investment horizons and the market for corporate control'. Defines the institution-level churn rate CR_i,t = sum_j |N_j,i,t P_j,t - N_j,i,t-1 P_j,t-1 - N_j,i,t-1 (P_j,t - P_j,t-1)| / sum_j (N_t P_t + N_t-1 P_t-1)/2 (Eq. 1; range [0,2]). The numerator subtracts N_{t-1}*dP, i.e. it equals |dN|*P_t: passive price drift is REMOVED from the numerator (share-based trade valued at current price). Drift only survives through the value-weighted denominator average. Firm-level 'investor turnover' = holding-weight-weighted average of holders' 4-quarter average churn (Eq. 2), computed on whole portfolio to avoid feedback from the target stock. Uses it for M&A outcomes (short-horizon holders -> lower premia, more value-destroying deals). Mean ownership-weighted horizon = LEVEL; no dispersion measure, no networks. Implication for pivot C: price-drift correction in turnover is already standard since 2005 (Gaspar churn, Carhart 1997, CRSP turnover); the 'value-weight vs share-based' contamination claim only novel for ratios using end-of-quarter value change as the numerator (as in the current paper's tau = 63/turnover), not for churn.

title: Life is Too Short? Bereaved Managers and Investment Decisions – Review of Finance
summary: Liu-Sulaeman-Shu-Yeung, Review of Finance 27(4):1373-1421 (2023). Parental death of 304 mutual fund managers (1999-2013) as exogenous shock; DiD finds bereaved managers act like quasi-indexers: lower tracking error, lower active share, lower idiosyncratic vol, higher beta, tilt to large stocks; effect stronger for unexpected deaths and single-manager funds; performance declines. Precedent for personal-event shocks to a fund's style, but the shock hits the focal manager's OWN risk preference, not a neighbour's; usable as an instrument for a neighbour's style/horizon shift (relevance: shifts toward indexing/lower turnover). Caveat: small sample, fund-level not 13F-institution-level, shock may shift turnover directly.

title: Mutual Fund Herding and the Impact
summary: Wermers (J. Finance 54(2):581-622, 1999; author PDF). Quarterly mutual-fund holdings 1975-1994. Adapts the Lakonishok-Shleifer-Vishny herding measure HM_i,t = |p_i,t - E[p_i,t]| - E|p_i,t - E[p_i,t]| (p = share of funds buying stock i in quarter t) and adds buy- vs sell-herding. Little herding in the average stock but much higher in small stocks and growth-oriented funds; stocks herds buy outperform stocks herds sell by 4 percent over the next six months, consistent with herding speeding price adjustment rather than destabilising. Canonical same-direction trading baseline: it measures coincidence of trade DIRECTION in a stock, not similarity of trading frequency or horizon, and not peer-driven adaptation; so pivot A (horizon contagion) is not pre-empted.

title: NBER WORKING PAPER SERIES
summary: Hong, Kubik, Stein (NBER WP 9711, 2003; later JF 2005): word-of-mouth/peer effects among US mutual fund managers. Fund manager more likely to hold/buy/sell a stock if OTHER managers in the same city (different fund family) hold/buy/sell it; robust to distance-to-stock (local preference) and style controls. Outcome variables: stock weight in focal fund's portfolio (holdings regressions) and quarterly change in weight/buys-sells (trades regressions); regressor = average weight of stock among other-family funds in same city. Magnitude: focal weight rises ~0.20 pct per 1 pct rise in same-city peers (coefficient ~0.2172). Identification: city*industry dummies, excluded same family, style controls; reflection-problem handled only by controls, no instruments. NOTHING on turnover, trading frequency or horizon: peer effect is on WHICH stock, not HOW OFTEN trade. Closest precedent to pivot A on method (peer-average regressors), but outcome differs.

summary: Greenwood, Landier & Thesmar (NBER WP 18537, 2012; JFE 2015) 'Vulnerable banks'. Model and application of fire-sale contagion through overlapping asset holdings: bank deleveraging at depressed prices spills over to banks with common exposures (European banks, 2010-11 sovereign crisis); measures vulnerability from holdings overlap and leverage; policy (mergers, equity injections). Result: illiquid volatile assets better spread across banks. Relevance: formal portfolio-overlap fire-sale network framework (banks), template for holdings-based spillover metrics; no horizon heterogeneity.

Evidence that own-history persistence dominates; supports trait view (cc-3 counter-explanation) and gives a peer-activity control precedent. Not a horizon/turnover peer-effect paper.

title: NBER WORKING PAPER SERIES
summary: Gilje-Gormley-Levit NBER WP 25644 (2019, JFE 2020 'Who's paying attention'). Argues asset-manager mergers (BlackRock-BGI 2009) need NOT raise managers' incentives to internalize externalities because investor attention is split; predicts 39-56% of stock pairs see DECLINE in incentives after BGI merger; empirical effect weaker after merger. Second critique (besides Lewellen-Lowry) of merger-as-exogenous-shock-to-common-ownership; shows the merger shock's treatment intensity is ambiguous, so a design must measure treatment as realized neighbour change in holdings.

title: NBER WORKING PAPER SERIES
summary: Coval & Stafford (2007 JFE; NBER WP 11357, 2005) 'Asset fire sales (and purchases) in equity markets'. Uses mutual fund flow-induced trades 1980-2003: funds in large outflow cut existing positions pro rata, creating price pressure in stocks held in common by distressed funds; prices fall then reverse (costs of fire sales), investors who trade against constrained funds earn large liquidity-provision returns; flow-driven trades are predictable so front-running is profitable. Mechanism rests on Shleifer-Vishny (1992) logic: buyers with highest valuation are similarly constrained peers. Relevance: foundational for common-ownership fire-sale channel (pivot B/overlap); identification = pro-rata flow-induced trades; no horizon-heterogeneity of holders and no horizon-based 'who absorbs the sale' split (the liquidity-provider is characterised as hedge funds/other funds, not by turnover horizon).

title: NBER WORKING PAPER SERIES
summary: Gabaix, Gopikrishnan, Plerou, Stanley (NBER w11722 / QJE 2006 'Institutional Investors and Stock Market Volatility'). Theory: very large institutions with Pareto-distributed size (exponent ~1) trade optimally given square-root-type price impact; yields power laws in returns (exponent ~3), volume (~1.5), price impact. Volatility spikes arise from large-investor trades without news. Heterogeneity is in SIZE not horizon; no horizon, no network. Background for 'granular' fragility; weak relevance to pivots A-E (cite only as size-based microfoundation alternative to the horizon/network story).

title: NBER WORKING PAPER SERIES
summary: Angrist (2014, NBER w19774) 'The Perils of Peer Effects'. Core results: (i) a regression of individual outcome on the group mean of the same outcome is vacuous: coefficient is exactly 1 (E[y mu_{y|z}]/V[mu_{y|z}]=1); with leave-out means it equals a function of the intraclass correlation, not behaviour. (ii) With predetermined covariates, 'peer effects' equal the gap between 2SLS (group dummies as instruments for own characteristic) and OLS; so a significant peer coefficient is a test of 2SLS=OLS, which can differ from measurement error, omitted variables, etc. (iii) Chance variation in group composition gives weak-IV bias; systematic variation removes weak IV but 2SLS>OLS from measurement error. (iv) Only randomized/quasi-experimental manipulation of peer characteristics is credible; such designs found little. Referee relevance: if horizon of institution i is regressed on mean horizon of overlap-neighbours, the result mechanically reflects clustering/grouping (leave-out mean induces mechanical negative bias, exclusion bias); a horizon-peer-effect claim needs exogenous variation in neighbours' horizons, not just a network regression.

title: NBER WORKING PAPER SERIES
summary: Caeyers & Fafchamps (NBER w22565, rev. 2020) 'Exclusion Bias in the Estimation of Peer Effects'. Exclusion bias: because i cannot be own peer, with selection-pool fixed effects (or small pools) i's characteristic is mechanically negatively correlated with mean of remaining peers; this downward bias applies to self-selected as well as random peers (first noted by Guryan et al. 2009; Angrist 2014). They derive exact bias formulas, combined reflection+exclusion bias, and a consistent estimator of endogenous and exogenous peer effects without instruments (needs restrictions on correlated effects), useful when peers are mutually exclusive equal-size groups. Also extends to autoregressive models (Nickell-type analogy). Referee relevance: with ~150 institutions per quarter, leave-own-out neighbour averages and quarter/institution fixed effects will induce exclusion bias (negative), pushing toward finding NO convergence; correct with their formulas or use non-overlapping neighbour constructions.

title: NBER WORKING PAPER SERIES
summary: Ouimet & Tate (NBER w24058, 2017; JF-type paper) 'Learning from Coworkers: Peer Effects on Individual Investment Decisions'. ESPP data, 500+ US firms: employees' decisions to participate in ESPP and to sell quickly respond to coworkers in the same CBSA; identification via metro-area x window fixed effects and firm x window fixed effects, i.e. same-firm, different-CBSA coworkers as comparison (absorbs local and firm-level common shocks). Peer influence stronger from similar and high-information peers; more susceptible: men, younger. Finance template for credible peer-effect design with fixed effects absorbing common shocks; relevant as an analogue for trading-horizon (sell speed) peer effects, though individual investors not institutions.

title: NBER WORKING PAPER SERIES
summary: Cochrane (NBER w28513, 2021) conceptual essay on portfolio theory for long-term investors: payout-stream view and general-equilibrium view of investors' differing preferences/risk-bearing roles. Theory/framing only; no horizon-heterogeneity measurement, 13F, or network content. LOW relevance to pivots A-E; at most a citation for why long-horizon investors should be liquidity providers (risk-bearing capacity differs by investor). Long (24k words) but not worth source-analyst.

title: NBER WORKING PAPER SERIES
summary: Ben-David, Franzoni, Moussawi, Sedunov (NBER WP 22247, rev. July 2020; published JF 2021). Large institutions' ownership predicts higher stock volatility, noisier prices and greater crisis fragility because institutions are 'granular': subunits (fund families) have correlated flows (Table 7: pairwise flow correlation higher within family) and similar holdings/trades, reducing idiosyncratic diversification. Table 8 Panel C: ownership by prior-quarter HIGH-TURNOVER top institutions (top quartile of min(Buys,Sells)/avg assets, Carhart 1997 turnover) has the largest relation with next-quarter volatility, interpreted as a trading-activity channel. Sample 1980Q1-2016Q4, stock and time FE, two-way clustering. Relevance: closest published use of turnover-sorted ownership LEVELS for volatility (level, not dispersion, of holder turnover, so pivot B's dispersion angle is not covered); turnover here is flow-based min(buys,sells)/assets, not price-drift-checked; correlated behaviour is within organisation, not horizon-based homophily across institutions. Also uses Ancerno trade data.

title: NBER WORKING PAPER SERIES
summary: Chinco & Ye (NBER WP 23650, 2017) 'Investment-Horizon Spillovers'. Wavelet decomposition of each stock's trading-volume variance into frequency components; stocks dominated by short-run volume fluctuations earn ~1%/month higher abnormal returns; short-run tilt changes rapidly month to month. Closest 'cross-horizon interaction within a stock' paper, but based on volume frequencies not 13F holder identities; no peer/network or horizon-adaptation element.

title: NBER WORKING PAPERS SERIES
summary: Lakonishok, Shleifer and Vishny, NBER WP 3846 (Sept 1991), 'Do institutional investors destabilize stock prices? Evidence on herding and feedback trading'; published as 'The impact of institutional trading on stock prices', J. Financial Economics 32(1):23-43 (1992). Working-paper version used because JFE page was bot-blocked. Data: quarterly holdings of 769 all-equity tax-exempt pension funds, 1985-1989. Defines the LSV herding measure (excess dispersion of buyer share across funds relative to expected under independence). Per search-snippet abstracts: mean herding .027, median .001 (virtually none in the typical stock), 6.1 percent in the smallest-cap quintile vs 1.6 percent in the largest; little evidence of positive-feedback trading and little evidence institutions destabilise. Canonical herding baseline; direction-of-trade based, no horizon or turnover dimension.

title: Network externalities in mutual funds
summary: Blocher (J. Financial Markets 30, 2016, 1-26; earlier 'Contagious Capital' 2012, 'Peer Effects in Mutual Funds' AEA 2014). Network of mutual funds linked by common holdings; flows into connected funds spill over via return-chasing investors; network externality 32-92% as large as lagged own flows; 1.5% quarterly excess return that reverses next year; robust to style and holdings-similarity specs. Outcomes: fund flows and returns. Portfolio-overlap network as peer group (relevant to pivot A/D), but peer variable is flows not horizon/turnover. Abstract page only; Darden/AEA PDFs 404/download-blocked.

title: Networks and Imitations in an Agent based Asset Market
summary: Masmoudi (SIMULTECH 2014): ABM where agents imitate forecasting RULES on small-world networks (rewiring probability varied); no investment horizon state, no similarity-based link formation, no empirical calibration.

title: Oldham 2019 Complexity full text (Wayback PDF): short-termism and dynamic investor network ABM
summary: Full text read: investor horizon is a fixed class (memory weight 0.95 vs 0.90) and never adapts; network rewires on performance toward class-specific 'Oracles', not horizon similarity; uncalibrated NetLogo ABM built on Harras-Sornette. Pivot E mechanism not pre-empted.

title: OUTSIDE AND INSIDE LIQUIDITY∗
summary: Bolton, Santos, Scheinkman 'Outside and Inside Liquidity' (QJE 2011; NBER w14867 2009, Columbia draft Apr 2010). Theory: short-run investors meet liquidity needs from cash reserves (inside) or by selling assets to long-run investors (outside liquidity); outside liquidity more efficient but asymmetric information causes early trading. Canonical theoretical anchor for 'long-horizon holders absorb short-horizon selling'; no data.

title: Outside and Inside Liquidity | NBER
summary: Bolton-Santos-Scheinkman NBER WP 14867 (2009), QJE 126:259-321 (2011). Model of liquidity demand: inside liquidity (cash) vs outside liquidity (asset sales); asymmetric information worsens with delay; immediate-trading vs delayed-trading equilibria, delayed Pareto superior; adverse selection can inefficiently accelerate liquidation. Relevance to pivot: theory of horizon of trading (when to trade) being an equilibrium object with strategic acceleration (strategic complementarity in early liquidation); supports pivot B (long-horizon holders as liquidity suppliers) more than A. Not a theory of horizon contagion; abstract-only.

title: Ownership Data on WRDS
summary: WRDS June 2020 slide deck: 13F scope (over $100m managers, quarterly, official list securities, $200,000/10,000-share thresholds), S34 missing entities (BlackRock 2018), Thomson SP quality issues around 2011, WRDS-SEC 13F from June 2013 with confidential-treatment flags. Vendor documentation, high reliability for data limits.

title: Page non trouvée
Peer effect of fund trading and the risk of individual stock
summary: Chen, Lin, Su, Yao, J Asian Econ 97 (2025): 'peer effect of fund trading behavior' in China raises individual-stock left-tail risk (signaling and liquidity channels). Peer effect here is trade-direction/herding-style, outcome is stock tail risk; NOT peer effect in fund turnover/horizon. Abstract-only (IDEAS). Adjacent to Pivot A and Pivot B (risk outcomes); does not pre-empt A.

title: Peer Effects in Networks: a Survey
summary: Bramoulle, Djebbari, Fortin (2020) 'Peer Effects in Networks: a Survey'. Reflection problem generally solved by network interactions absent correlated effects; microfoundations (why peers matter) generally not identified. Four approaches to correlated effects/network endogeneity: random peers, random shocks (randomized treatment valid even with endogenous network if network not affected by treatment), structural endogeneity (joint network-formation + outcome model, e.g., Goldsmith-Pinkham & Imbens 2013 with observed + unobserved homophily in link formation), and panel data (underdeveloped). Warning: peers-of-peers instruments are invalid if the network is mismeasured, since 'friends of friends who are not friends' may be direct peers (Blume et al. 2015), and invalid in sampled networks (Chandrasekhar & Lewis 2016, Prop 3.4); clustering/transitivity of real networks makes this serious. Key checklist for referee objections to a horizon peer-effect design.

title: PRELIMINARY PROOF
summary: Chamley (Theoretical Economics 2 (2007) 1-27) 'Complementarities in information acquisition with short-term trades'. Short-term-profit traders: strategic complementarities in acquiring private information (info is more valuable when more agents are informed); continuum/multiple equilibria; two regimes (trading frenzies). Another formal source of complementarity tied to short horizons (distinct from FSS); supports 'horizon complementarity' mechanism.

title: Pricing Liquidity Risk with Heterogeneous Investment
summary: Beber, Driessen, Tuijp (Oct 2012 draft, later JF-adjacent working paper) equilibrium model: stochastic transaction costs plus investors with heterogeneous exogenous horizons; short-horizon investors hold only liquid assets, so illiquid-asset liquidity premia depend on the horizon distribution (heterogeneity) and liquid/illiquid correlation. Estimated on cross-section of US stocks; fits average returns better than liquidity-CAPM and gives larger liquidity premia. Horizons are exogenous/static - no network, no adaptation, no stability or volatility outcome. Relevant for (a) theory of horizon heterogeneity and as precedent that horizon DISTRIBUTION (not level) matters for pricing (pivot B motivation), but cross-sectional pricing not fragility.

title: RESEARCH ARTICLE
summary: Delpini, Battiston, Caldarelli, Riccaboni (PLoS ONE 2019) 'Systemic risk from investment similarities': bipartite US mutual fund-asset network through GFC; overlap far more likely than random; similarity-based systemic risk. No horizon/turnover typology. Closeness to D: ADJACENT (overlap network), no horizon dimension.

title: ScholarWorks :: Institutional investor heterogeneity and market price dynamics: Evidence from investment horizon and portfolio concentration
summary: Kim, Kim, Joe, Oh (J Financial Markets 54, 2021, doi 10.1016/j.finmar.2020.100604). Abstract only via Korea Univ ScholarWorks (full text paywalled; no open copy found, core.ac.uk blocked). Two-way classification of institutions by investment horizon x portfolio concentration; short horizon and high concentration both proxy informational advantage; concentrated vs diversified institutions differ even at equal horizon. Institution-TYPE classification effect on price dynamics, not within-stock horizon dispersion or stress absorption. Adjacent.
