Shareholder Trading Practices and Corporate Investment Horizons | NBER
summary: Froot-Perold-Stein NBER WP 3638 (1991, JACF 1992). Examines shareholder turnover/trading practices (excess volatility, institutional turnover) and corporate investment horizons; data on US vs other-country institutional turnover. Background for horizon-as-trait-of-institution and the claim that high turnover is associated with non-fundamental-trading-driven volatility. Abstract-only.

title: Similar Investors1
summary: Georg, Pierret, Steffen, 'Similar Investors' (slides from BoE/CEPR/Imperial/LSE conference Oct 2019; later versions SSRN 3250826 / 5536678, AEA 2024 program, AFA listing). US prime money market funds (213 funds, 295 issuers): investors who trade an asset care about who else holds it. Fund-by-issuer portfolio similarity = 100*(1 - Euclidean distance of portfolio shares/sqrt2), weighted by other funds' share of the issuer's funding. H1: funds reduce exposure to an issuer when they are similar to its other funds' holders (fire-sale/joint-liquidation-cost avoidance, Wagner 2012 diversification-diversity trade-off); H2: issuers with a similar investor base face higher funding liquidity risk. Identification via an instrument based on variation in similarity from other funds' idiosyncratic redemptions; effect stronger for ex-post illiquid securities, illiquid/diversified funds and active institutional funds. Relevance: closest published template for (a) a holder-base similarity measure per stock/issuer and (b) an IV for peer overlap shocks (supports pivot A/B identification design), but similarity is holdings-based, NOT horizon-based; MMFs, not equities; no horizon/turnover (zero hits). Note: AEA and SSRN pages were blocked; this note is from the slide deck only.

title: Social Impact at Kellogg  |  J.L. Kellogg School of Management at Northwestern University
summary: Kellogg research brief on Starks-Venkat-Zhu 'Corporate ESG Profiles and Investor Horizons' (JF 81(2), Apr 2026, 603-642 per MetaTOC; Moskowitz Prize 2021). 13F institutions classed by horizon; long-term investors tilt toward high-ESG firms and are more patient after poor returns; FTSE4Good inclusion attracts long-horizon holders. Level of horizon, not dispersion or contagion; recent JF use of holdings-based horizon -> shows horizon measurement is publishable at top journals.

title: Social Interaction Intensity
summary: Gelman, Hirshleifer, Levi, Reiter-Gavish, 'Social Interaction Intensity and Investor Behavior' (NBER w32772 Aug 2024; Feb 2025 version; listed ABFER 2025). This is the 'ABFER 2025 social interaction and trading volume' paper. Outcome: individual investors' buying sensitivity to past buys, trading volume sensitivity, portfolio riskiness; stock-level volume and retail ownership. Peer definition: local community exposure to soccer-game-driven social interaction intensity (Israel). Data: Israeli bank, 131,003 retail accounts; identification: exogenous timing of local soccer games. RETAIL only, volume/riskiness sensitivity to peers' past buys; no institutions, no horizon/turnover convergence, no 13F. Closeness to pivot A: ADJACENT (retail trading-volume peer effect), not a near-duplicate.

title: Socially connected fund managers share investment ideas
summary: LSE Business Review blog summary of Pool, Stoffman, Yonker (2016); weak/derivative, neighbours have more similar portfolios.

title: Statistically validated network of portfolio overlaps and systemic risk - PMC
summary: Gualdi, Cimini, Primicerio, Di Clemente, Challet (Scientific Reports 2016, 6:39467). Statistically validated network of portfolio overlaps among SEC 13F institutions 1999-2013 using a Bipartite Configuration Model null (degrees of institutions and securities fixed in expectation); the share of validated links (significant overlaps) rises before the 2007-08 crisis, peaks at the crisis, drops in 2008 and rises again to a 2013 maximum; they argue it measures fire-sale systemic risk; validated links indicate amplified losses in bear markets and gains in bull markets. Relevance: standard method for building 13F co-holding networks that control for portfolio size/diversification and stock popularity; a defensible null for pivot D (the current paper's raw cosine similarity is confounded by size and by popular stocks; BiCM-validated links or degree-preserving permutation would answer the obvious referee objection). No horizon/turnover attributes of nodes (grep: zero hits). Page carries unrelated NIH banner boilerplate, ignorable.

title: Stock price fragility$
summary: Greenwood & Thesmar (2011 JFE) 'Stock price fragility'. Defines asset fragility as susceptibility to non-fundamental demand shifts; depends on (i) concentrated ownership and (ii) owners' correlated or volatile liquidity (flow) shocks. Fragility = expected volatility of ownership-weighted flow-driven demand, computed from mutual fund holdings 1990-2007, decomposing trades into active rebalancing vs flow-driven trading (eq. 4). Fragility predicts total and idiosyncratic volatility (univariate R2 about 8%) beyond known controls even though mutual funds own only ~15% of shares of median stock. Extensions: co-fragility predicts comovement (via correlated flows between owners' funds) and fragility betas; fragility effect is weaker where hedge funds (arbitrageurs) trade against flow shocks and stronger where they trade with them. Notes it differs from fraction-of-institutional-ownership results (Sias 1996, Bushee-Noe 2000). Relevance for pivot B: this is the central prior art on ownership-composition-as-volatility predictor; it uses the flow-volatility/correlation of owners, NOT holder-horizon dispersion; it already tests liquidity-provision by arbitrageurs (hedge funds) inside the same stock. Horizon dispersion would need to be positioned as an increment over fragility (control for it). Fetched via HBS-hosted published-layout PDF (DOI link blocked by ScienceDirect bot wall).

title: Stock price fragility$
summary: Greenwood & Thesmar (JFE 102, 2011, 471-490). Defines a stock as fragile if its owners face correlated or volatile liquidity (flow) shocks or ownership is concentrated: fragility = w'Omega w, where w = owner weights and Omega = conditional variance-covariance matrix of owners' flow shocks; applied to US mutual-fund ownership; fragility strongly predicts price volatility and extends to comovement and (per abstract) issuance/return forecasts. Ownership heterogeneity enters through the covariance of holders' flows (estimated from fund-flow history), NOT through dispersion of holder turnover/horizon. Key template for pivot B: a horizon-dispersion measure would need to be shown to add to or differ from the flow-covariance fragility measure. Also fed by flow-driven fragility literature (d).

title: Systemic risk from investment similarities - PMC
summary: Delpini, Battiston, Caldarelli & Riccaboni (2019 PLoS ONE 14(5):e0217141) 'Systemic risk from investment similarities'. Bipartite network of US mutual fund portfolios (CRSP MF holdings) through the GFC; cosine similarity of portfolios; finds portfolios became more diversified and less similar during crisis but overlap far above random-allocation null; adds a distress-propagation model in which a fund imitates the liquidations of its most similar fund with probability equal to their cosine similarity (an explicit similarity-weighted imitation/contagion rule). Diversification and similarity trade off in systemic risk. Relevance: close prior art for (i) cosine portfolio similarity networks of funds and (ii) similarity-weighted imitation contagion in simulation; but no investor horizon, no peer-effect econometrics, not 13F. Journal-version of arXiv 1801.02205.

title: The contagion effect of heterogeneous investor groups - PMC
summary: PLOS ONE 2023: Korean exchange data 2002-2018, variance-decomposition connectedness among investor GROUPS (retail, institutions, foreigners); retail pivotal in propagation. Group-level trading-flow connectedness, not horizon contagion. Low relevance, tagged for completeness.

title: The Impact of Manager Changes on Fund
The influence of the social networks of fund managers on the herding behavior of SIFs in China | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications
summary: Humanities Soc Sci Commun 2023: Chinese fund managers' social-network size (not constraint) lowers fund herding measured by CSAD. Herding in return dispersion, network is manager biography ties; no turnover/horizon. Adjacent only.

title: The Information in Asset Fire Sales
summary: Huang, Ringgenberg, Zhang (Management Science 69(9):5066-5086, 2023). Mutual fund fire sales: price pressure driven by asymmetric information; separates expected vs unexpected trades. Adjacent: fire-sale mechanics, no horizon heterogeneity.

title: THE JOURNAL OF FINANCE • VOL. LXIX, NO. 3 • JUNE 2014
summary: Anton & Polk (2014 JF) 'Connected Stocks'. Builds stock-pair connectedness from common active mutual fund owners (share of each stock's market cap owned by shared funds); shared ownership forecasts excess return correlation after four-factor, industry/size/BM/momentum and analyst-coverage controls (big stocks only). Causal evidence from the 2003 mutual-fund trading scandal (outflows from implicated funds give exogenous variation in common ownership). Effect stronger when common owners face large flows (in or out) and for low-float stocks. Predicted variation in four-factor residual correlation ranges -0.046 to 0.029. Cross-stock reversal strategy; hedge-fund index returns covary negatively with it. Relevance: canonical stock-network from overlap via common owners; flow-driven channel only, NO investor horizon/turnover dimension and no heterogeneity-of-holders measure. Cites Greenwood-Thesmar co-fragility. Closest-paper for pivot A/D network construction but not horizon.

title: The Long and The Short: Portfolio Turnover Ratios &
summary: Tucker (J. Corp. Law 43:3, 2018) 'The Long and the Short: Portfolio Turnover Ratios & Mutual Fund Investment Time Horizons'. Mutual-fund 2005-15 data: PTR-implied holding periods 15-17 months, no decline. Compares PTR with Duration, Churn Rate (holding ~10-12 months, more volatile) and Champagne et al. 'Modified Turnover' MT = 0.5 * sum |w_obs - w_buy&hold|, which explicitly strips 'mechanical portfolio adjustments driven by stock price fluctuations' (w_BH = w_{t-1} (1+R_i)/(1+R_BH)). Legal-scholarship venue (low authority for econ claims) but documents that price-drift-neutral turnover (MT, Champagne-Karoui-Patel) exists in the mutual-fund literature: pre-empts pivot C as a pure novelty claim; residual angle is 13F-wide, quantifying how drift contaminates horizon-vs-VIX / diversity-index results.

title:
The more we know, the less we agree: A test of the trading horizon heterogeneity theory
      -  Macquarie University
summary: Dai, Parwada, Winchester, Zhang (Financial Review 57(1):45-67, 2022) tests Kondor (RES 2012) trading-horizon heterogeneity theory with 13F: a LARGER PROPORTION of short-term investors (level share) raises post-earnings-announcement abnormal volume and return volatility; Russell 1000/2000 reconstitution RDD identification. Level of short-horizon share, not dispersion; event-window volatility, not crash/stress. Adjacent to pivot B (horizon mix -> volatility).

title: The Network of U.S. Mutual Fund Investments:
summary: Delpini et al. (arXiv 1801.02205 v1, Jan 2018) working-paper version of 'Systemic risk from investment similarities': bipartite network of US mutual fund portfolios and assets through GFC; diversification vs similarity; simplified shock propagation model shows a systemic-risk component from portfolio similarity ('diversification may even increase systemic risk when funds diversify in the same way'). Duplicate of the PLoS ONE version; cite the journal version. No horizon dimension.

title: The Network of U.S. Mutual Fund Investments:
summary: Fricke/Delpini-type bipartite US mutual fund network 2005-2010 (arXiv 1801.02205): portfolio similarity (Jaccard x weights) and fragility through the GFC; community structure shows funds clustering into groups with similar portfolios. Does NOT sort similarity by turnover/horizon; so no prior art for horizon-sorted overlap.

title: The People in Your Neighborhood: Social Interactions and Mutual Fund Portfolios
summary: Pool, Stoffman, Yonker (JF 70(6) 2015, 2679-2732; IDEAS abstract only, publisher full text blocked). Fund managers' residential address histories from public records; neighbours (same neighborhood) have more similar holdings and trades than same-city different-neighborhood managers; larger for same ethnicity; not explained by preferences; long-short of neighbours' buys minus sells earns positive risk-adjusted returns. Outcome variables: holdings overlap/similarity (pairwise fund-pair), trade similarity, performance of copied trades. No turnover/horizon outcome reported in abstract. Pairwise similarity design is the closest analogue to the paper's 'horizon-proximity vs cosine similarity' fact (D) but runs the other way (social tie -> similar holdings).

title: The People in Your Neighborhood: Social Interactions and Mutual Fund Portfolios - Noah Stoffman
summary: Pool, Stoffman, Yonker (JF 2015, 70(6):2679-2732) -- abstract page only (139 words fetched). Socially connected fund managers (same neighbourhood) have more similar holdings and trades; overlap is higher for same-neighbourhood than same-city-different-neighbourhood pairs, larger with shared ethnic background, not explained by preferences; neighbour-trade long-short strategy earns positive risk-adjusted returns; tests disentangle social interaction from community effects. Relevance: canonical peer-network-to-portfolio-similarity result for mutual funds and the identification template (neighbourhood vs city) for peer effects in fund behaviour; no horizon or turnover outcome. Shows that 'similar holdings among connected managers' is established; the missing piece for pivot A is peer effects in horizon/turnover rather than holdings.

The role of institutional investors in propagating the crisis of 2007-2008∗
summary: Manconi, Massa & Yasuda (2012 JFE 104:491-518). Bond-holdings data; funds facing redemptions and holding illiquid securitized bonds sold liquid corporate bonds, propagating the 2007-08 crisis; uses fund turnover and flow volatility as proxies for investors' liquidity needs/ investor horizon (higher-turnover funds matched with shorter-horizon investors, more liquidity risk); high turnover / high flow-volatility funds liquidated more. Relevance: a precedent that fund turnover (a horizon proxy) predicts fire-sale behaviour and cross-asset contagion; it is fund-level (clientele), not stock-level holder-horizon dispersion, and bond-focused. Useful for pivot B and for the turnover-as-horizon-proxy measurement debate.

title: The short-termism trap: Catering to informed investors with limited horizons
summary: Dow-Han-Sangiorgi, JFE 159 (2024) 103884 (RePEc record). Theory: informed investors with limited horizons induce firms to shorten project maturity; feedback among firms; long-term investors only partly alleviate. Horizon is a firm-side/corporate-policy channel, not holdings-based measurement or network. Related to pivot B only as theory of horizon mix mattering.

title: Thinking ahead for Europe
summary: Stahel (ECMI WP 13, Nov 2021), Strategic Complementarity among Investors with Overlapping Portfolios. Tests whether run-like outflow behaviour is a general feature of investors with overlapping portfolios competing for finite market liquidity, not specific to mutual-fund NAV redemption: uses separately managed accounts 2000-2021 (investors own assets directly, NAV/common-pool channel off). Flow-performance relation is concave for overlapping portfolios holding less liquid assets; outflow sensitivity to underperformance rises in market illiquidity and for less liquid portfolios; weaker for investors with large account holdings (internalise own price impact). Relevance: overlap as the channel for strategic complementarity in selling (supports pivot B logic that who else holds a stock matters in stress); no horizon/turnover variable. Clientele is retail/SMA investors, not 13F institutions.

title: TI 2005-056/1
summary: Hommes (2006) Handbook of Computational Economics ch.23 (TI 05-056/1): survey of stylized dynamic heterogeneous agent models (Brock-Hommes switching, chartist/fundamentalist), survey/experimental evidence on horizon-dependent expectations (extrapolative at short, mean-reverting at long horizons). Agent type switching is driven by past performance (discrete choice), not by neighbours' horizons; network/social interaction treated peripherally. Reference survey for the HAM tradition; shows adaptation-by-performance is the standard mechanism.

title: University of California
summary: Wool (UCLA PhD dissertation 2013, supervisor Roll) 'Essays Concerning the Network Structure of Mutual Fund Holdings and the Behavior of Institutional Investors', FULL TEXT. Ch1: stock centrality in fund-stock bipartite graph predicts returns (+4.1%/yr for stocks moving toward the center); discusses Hong-Kubik-Stein, Blocher (holdings-overlap peers). Ch on 13(d). Uses stock TURNOVER only as control. Closeness to A and D: NONE (no horizon convergence, no horizon-similarity test).

title: Unraveling Peers and Peer Eﬀects:
summary: M. Jackson discussion of Goldsmith-Pinkham & Imbens (2013) 'Social Networks and the Identification of Peer Effects'. Lists identification hazards: endogenous networks/homophily (linked individuals alike in observed AND unobserved traits, so similarity may be mistaken for influence), computational burden of endogenous-network models (Chandrasekhar & Jackson 2012), measurement error in network ties, and timing. Notes that fitted network-formation model on Add Health shows strong homophily on observed traits. Short discussion piece (3k words); useful for the homophily-vs-influence confound central to the horizon-homophily/convergence design.

title: w o r k i n g
summary: Heimer (FRB Cleveland WP 13-14, Oct 2013; JEBO 107(B) 2014) 'Friends Do Let Friends Buy Stocks Actively' FULL TEXT. Outcome: household active-management proxies (portfolio turnover variables: buying/selling assets) from Consumer Expenditure Survey; peer/sociability proxy = expenditure items implying social activity; logistic regressions of active management on sociability, conditional on participation; falsification with unrelated expenditure. Correlational, households, no network peers, no institutions. Closeness to A: ADJACENT (turnover/active-trading as outcome, social channel), but retail, survey, no peer-network identification.

title: Which Investors Matter for Equity Valuations and Expected Returns? | NBER
summary: Koijen-Richmond-Yogo (NBER w27402; Review of Economic Studies 91(4), 2024, 2387-2424). Demand-system (latent-demand) approach to 13F holdings: per dollar of assets hedge funds and small active advisors move prices most; long-horizon investors (pensions, insurers) least. Relevant to pivot B (holder-type heterogeneity and price impact) but heterogeneity is by institution type, not within-stock horizon dispersion. Needed as comparison design.

title: Why is Persistent Mutual Fund Performance so Difficult to Achieve?
Working Paper 2515
summary: Ozdagli-Ryfe, Dallas Fed WP 2515r1 (Jun 2025): insurers sharing asset managers hold more similar corporate-bond portfolios and trades; ties portfolio similarity to financial stability. Close analogue to D/A (similarity from a common-driver channel) and a warning that similarity can reflect common managers/advisors, not homophily; bond-side evidence relevant to N-PORT extension.

title: WORKING PAPER NO. 276
summary: Cespa-Vives (CSEF WP 276, 2011; later JF/ CEPR DP8303 'Higher order expectations, illiquidity and short-term trading'). Theory: when traders have different trading frequencies/horizons, prices reflect higher-order expectations; multiple equilibria ranked by liquidity and informational efficiency; with short-term agents prices over-rely on public information, market illiquid, informed investors do not supply liquidity; high-liquidity equilibrium with high informational trading. Positive feedback loop across trading dates drives multiplicity. Gives mechanism for horizon complementarity (a trader's horizon matters because of others' horizons) and for pivot B: horizon mix of holders determines liquidity and whether informed long-horizon investors act as liquidity suppliers.

title: Working Paper Series
summary: Timmer (ESRB WP 18, July 2016; published JFE 129(2):268-286, 2018) 'Cyclical investment behavior across financial institutions'. German Securities Holdings Statistics (security-by-institution, debt securities). Banks and investment funds trade PROCYCLICALLY in response to security-level price changes (sell discounts/falling prices, buy premium/rising), insurers and pension funds trade COUNTERCYCLICALLY (buy when prices fall); balance-sheet constraints within sector explain procyclicality. Sorting is by institution TYPE, not measured horizon; debt not equity; Germany; no dispersion/horizon-mix outcome, no stock volatility. Supports the sign (long-horizon-type liquidity provision) but is adjacent to pivot B, not a within-stock horizon-absorption test on US equities.

note_id: 和而不群还是卓尔不群基于基金网络信息使用的视角
title: “和而不群”还是“卓尔不群”?——基于基金网络信息使用的视角
summary: Chinese (Journal of Financial Research-type page): fund network built from heavy-holdings overlap; 'network information use' = deviation of a fund's trades from avg trades of network peers. Funds using less network info outperform; mover (manager-change) evidence says network-info use is more tied to manager traits than fund traits (portable-manager-trait result for peer-trade deviation, not turnover). Relevant to cc-1 (peer convergence in trades) and cc-3 (trait portability). Does not regress turnover/horizon on peers.

note_id: 基金经理更换股票联动与股票价格
title: 基金经理更换、股票联动与股票价格
summary: Chinese: fund manager changes break stock co-movement within co-held portfolios (new manager rebuilds portfolio; hedge portfolio earns 0.1% daily excess return; 2008-2014 China). Shows manager change = portfolio overhaul event, supporting the manager-departure event design but also the point that manager changes are not exogenous to holdings. No turnover regression on peers.

note_id: 机构投资者理性泡沫骑乘及其动因探究
title: 机构投资者理性泡沫骑乘及其动因探究
summary: Chen Guojin et al., China Industrial Economics 2021 (Chinese): institutions ride bubbles (raise holdings of high crash-probability stocks, exit before peak); drivers = inside information and institutional peer effect (同群效应). Peer group = Louvain communities in the institutions' holdings network; peer variable = value-weighted avg crash-probability of the community's holdings. Closest methodological precedent for a co-holding-network peer effect in China, but the peer-influenced behavior is bubble-riding (portfolio exposure), not turnover/horizon; no neighbour-excluding-holdings construction, so mechanical overlap contamination is not addressed. Partial pre-emption of the generic estimand, not of A.
